7-1.title: Minerals
7-1.learn:
KEY IDEAS

A mineral is a naturally formed SOLID with a specific chemical makeup and an orderly CRYSTAL pattern inside. (Minerals are not made by living things and are not man-made.)

Scientists identify minerals by their PROPERTIES:
- Color: what color it appears (but color alone can be misleading).
- Hardness: how easily it can be scratched (measured on the Mohs scale).
- Luster: how shiny or dull it looks (metallic vs. nonmetallic).
- Streak: the color of the powder it leaves when scraped on a tile.

Minerals are the building blocks of ROCKS, and we use them in everyday items.

Example 1 — Streak vs. color
Two minerals may look the same color, but their STREAK (powder color) can be different, helping tell them apart.

Example 2 — Hardness test
A harder mineral can scratch a softer one. Diamond is the hardest mineral, so it can scratch nearly anything.

Example 3 — Is it a mineral?
A salt crystal is a mineral (natural solid, orderly crystal pattern). Sugar from a plant or a plastic bead is NOT a mineral, because minerals must form naturally and not from living things.

questions.explanation: Minerals are natural solids with a specific chemical makeup and an orderly crystal pattern inside.

questions.explanation: A natural quartz crystal is a mineral. Plastic and glass are man-made, and sugar comes from a living thing.

choices.B: Mineral B is harder than Mineral A

choices.B: A substance made by a living plant

questions.explanation: Minerals must form naturally and not come from living things, so a substance made by a plant is not a mineral.

questions.explanation: Testing color, hardness, luster, and streak helps a scientist identify which mineral a sample is.

7-2.title: Rocks and How They Form
7-2.learn:
KEY IDEAS

Rocks are made of one or more minerals. There are three main types, grouped by how they form:
- Igneous rock forms when melted rock (magma or lava) COOLS and hardens. (Example: granite, basalt.)
- Sedimentary rock forms when bits of rock and sand get PRESSED and CEMENTED together in layers. (Example: sandstone, limestone.)
- Metamorphic rock forms when HEAT and PRESSURE change an existing rock WITHOUT melting it. (Example: marble from limestone, slate from shale.)

The type of rock tells a story about how and where it formed.

Example 1 — Cooled lava
When lava from a volcano cools and hardens, it forms igneous rock.

Example 2 — Layers at the bottom of a lake
Sand and mud settle in layers, then get pressed and cemented into sedimentary rock.

Example 3 — Squeezed and heated
When limestone is heated and squeezed deep underground (without melting), it becomes the metamorphic rock marble.

questions.explanation: Cooled, hardened lava forms igneous rock.

questions.explanation: Marble forms from limestone changed by heat and pressure, so it is a metamorphic rock.

7-3.title: The Rock Cycle
7-3.learn:
KEY IDEAS

The rock cycle is the never-ending loop in which rocks slowly change from one type to another over millions of years. Any rock can become any other type.

Main processes that change rocks:
- Heat and pressure → turn rock into METAMORPHIC rock.
- Melting → turns rock into magma, which cools into IGNEOUS rock.
- Weathering and erosion → break rock into sediment, which gets pressed into SEDIMENTARY rock.

Example 1 — Igneous to sedimentary
An igneous rock can be weathered into tiny pieces (sediment), which are then pressed and cemented into sedimentary rock.

Example 2 — Any to igneous
Any rock that gets hot enough to MELT becomes magma; when it cools, it forms igneous rock.

Example 3 — Slow change
The rock cycle takes a very long time — usually millions of years — as rocks melt, break down, or get squeezed into new forms.

questions.question: The rock cycle describes how rocks

choices.A: slowly change from one type to another over time

questions.explanation: The rock cycle is the slow, ongoing change of rocks from one type to another.

questions.question: Melting a rock and letting the magma cool forms which type of rock?
questions.explanation: Melted rock that cools and hardens forms igneous rock.

questions.question: Heat and pressure (without melting) change a rock into
questions.explanation: Heat and pressure without melting turn a rock into metamorphic rock.

questions.question: Weathering breaks rock into small pieces called
questions.explanation: Weathering breaks rock into sediment, which can later form sedimentary rock.

questions.question: About how long does the rock cycle usually take to change rocks?
questions.explanation: The rock cycle usually takes millions of years.

questions.question: An igneous rock is broken into sediment, then pressed and cemented. It becomes a
questions.explanation: Sediment that is pressed and cemented becomes a sedimentary rock.

questions.question: Which statement about the rock cycle is TRUE?

choices.B: Any rock type can eventually become any other type

questions.explanation: In the rock cycle, any rock can eventually become any other type over time.

questions.question: A sedimentary rock is buried deep and squeezed by heat and pressure. It changes into
questions.explanation: Heat and pressure change the sedimentary rock into metamorphic rock without melting it.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly shows part of the rock cycle?

choices.A: Magma cools into igneous rock, which weathers into sediment
choices.B: Sediment melts directly into metamorphic rock
choices.C: Metamorphic rock turns instantly into a mineral
choices.D: Igneous rock turns into a living thing

questions.explanation: Magma cools to form igneous rock, which can then weather into sediment, part of the rock cycle.

questions.question: What process is needed to turn any rock into igneous rock?
questions.explanation: To form igneous rock, a rock must melt into magma and then cool and harden.
